opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really important point, and it's one we tried to be careful about. In the paper, we studied a fairly controlled, somewhat stripped-down RAG setup. You take a model, you retrieve a set of documents, you put them into the context, and then you look at how the model's behavior changes, particularly around safety. We did that deliberately, because if you want to isolate the effect of retrieval itself, you need to hold a lot of other things constant.

But that's not what a production system at a company actually looks like. In industry, and certainly at a place like Bloomberg, a deployed RAG system has many more layers around it. You have input classifiers and guardrails that screen the query before it ever reaches the model. You have curated, vetted document collections rather than arbitrary web content. There's often filtering on the retrieved content, post-generation checks, domain-specific policies, and sometimes human review. Each of those components changes the risk profile considerably.

So I don't want anyone to walk away thinking, "RAG systems in the wild are unsafe, full stop." That's not the claim. The claim is more specific and, I think, more useful: adding retrieval to a model can change its safety behavior in ways people don't expect, sometimes making a model that looks safe in isolation behave less safely once you give it documents. A lot of practitioners assume retrieval makes things safer because you're grounding the model in trusted sources, and our results suggest you can't take that for granted.

The practical takeaway is that safety evaluation has to happen on the system as it's actually deployed, not just on the base model. If you evaluate a model, find it refuses harmful requests, and then wrap it in a RAG pipeline, you can't assume those properties carry over. You need to re-test in the configuration you're shipping, ideally with red-teaming that reflects your domain and your users.

So distinguishing the two matters both for honesty about what our experiments show and for making the finding actionable. It's a signal to look closely at your own pipeline, not a verdict on every RAG deployment out there.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the paper’s controlled retrieval-and-generation setup with deployed industry systems, which add stages such as input classifiers, curated document collections, content filtering, post-generation checks, policies, and human review.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I really want to be careful about, because I think it's easy for a headline like "RAG makes models less safe" to get picked up and applied to systems it doesn't actually describe.

What we studied in the paper is a very stripped-down setup. You take a model, you retrieve a set of documents, you put them in the context window, and you ask the model to answer. That's it. No input guardrails, no output filtering, no retrieval-side classifiers, no system-level policies about what sources are allowed. We did that deliberately, because we wanted to isolate the question: what does the mere presence of retrieved context do to the model's safety behavior? And the finding was that even with benign, totally innocuous documents, the model becomes measurably more willing to produce unsafe outputs than it is in the plain, no-retrieval setting. That's a statement about the model itself, about how the fine-tuning for safety interacts with long contexts and with the instruction to ground your answer in the documents.

Now, the systems people actually deploy in industry look very different. In a production setting at a place like Bloomberg, retrieval is one component inside a much larger pipeline. You've got controls on which corpora you retrieve from, you've got classifiers before and after the model, you often have task-specific constraints, and you've got monitoring on top of all of it. So if you read our paper and conclude that a deployed RAG product has the vulnerabilities we measured at the same rates, that's just not a valid inference. The surrounding system might fully compensate for the effect, or it might not, and you'd have to test that specific system to know.

The reason I think the distinction matters in both directions, though, is this. On one side, I don't want people to over-generalize and panic about production systems based on a controlled experiment. But on the other side, I also don't want people to dismiss the finding because "well, we have guardrails." The point of the paper is that the guardrails that come baked into the model, the ones you get from the model provider's safety training, were largely evaluated in a no-context, single-turn chat setting. Our result says that those assurances don't automatically transfer once you add retrieval. So if you're building a RAG system and you're relying on the model's built-in safety as one of your layers, you should know that layer is weaker than you probably assumed, and you need to evaluate your system in its actual deployed configuration rather than trusting the model card.

So the distinction is really about being precise about what claim the evidence supports. The experiment tells you something real about the model. It doesn't tell you the risk of any particular product, and anyone building one of those products needs to run their own red teaming in context.

r001.rationale: The response describes the paper’s setup as retrieving documents and placing them in the model’s context, then contrasts it with industry systems that add corpus controls, classifiers, task-specific constraints, and monitoring.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s important because RAG describes a pretty broad range of systems. In a paper, you typically study a particular configuration under controlled conditions: how you retrieve information, what you give the model, and how you evaluate its response. That lets you isolate a question, but it also limits how broadly you can interpret the findings.

An industry system might include query rewriting, multiple retrieval steps, reranking, or additional checks on the generated answer. Those choices can substantially change its behavior. So we should be precise about what our results establish for the setup we studied, rather than treating them as a conclusion about every system that uses retrieval. The distinction helps practitioners understand which findings might transfer to their application and which they need to test themselves.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the paper’s controlled retrieval-and-generation setup with industry systems that may add query rewriting, multiple retrieval steps, reranking, and answer checks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s important because RAG describes a whole family of systems, and the particular setup you study affects what you can conclude. In a paper, you typically simplify things so you can isolate a question and understand what’s driving the results. An industry system might have additional retrieval steps, filtering, reranking, or other components that change what information actually reaches the model.

So the distinction is really about the scope of the claims. A failure in the setup we study can tell us something useful about how a model uses retrieved information, but it doesn’t automatically mean every production RAG system will fail in the same way. You have to connect the finding back to the choices made in that particular system.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the paper’s simplified setup with industry systems that may add retrieval, filtering, reranking, and other processing components.
